analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal minimum wage and overtime exemption for home care workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 83 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes the Fair Labor Standards Act so that home health aides and personal care aides are covered by the federal minimum wage and overtime pay rules, which they are currently exempt from under a decades-old carve-out for "companionship" and casual domestic work. It keeps only true casual babysitting exempt — occasional, irregular childcare in the child's own home by someone whose vocation is not babysitting. Trained caregivers such as nurses and home care workers would lose the exemption and become entitled to at least the federal minimum wage and time-and-a-half after 40 hours a week.
analysis.who_benefits: Home care workers — home health aides and personal care aides, most of whom are women and many of whom are immigrants — would gain a federal right to minimum wage and overtime pay for all hours worked. Workers who now routinely work 50 or 60 hours a week at straight time, or below minimum wage once unpaid travel between clients and on-call time are counted, would see their paychecks rise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home health and personal care aides

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the FLSA exemption for domestic service employees, so caregiving workers would be covered by the federal minimum wage and overtime requirements just like most other workers.

It also repeals the separate exemption for providers of companionship services (FLSA section 13(b)(21)), closing the loophole under which home care agencies are not required to pay overtime for aides.

Only casual babysitting — irregular or intermittent childcare in the child's own home by someone whose vocation is not babysitting, with no more than 20 percent of hours spent on other household work — would remain exempt, so occasional sitters are not pulled into wage-and-hour litigation.

analysis.who_pays: Home care agencies that employ aides would bear higher payroll costs, and those costs would flow to families who pay for care out of pocket and to Medicaid and other public programs that fund most home care. Some agencies could respond by cutting hours, raising prices, or reducing the number of billable care hours they offer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Home care agencies and care funders

drawbacks.text: Higher labor costs would land on home care agencies, families paying privately, and Medicaid programs; agencies might respond by cutting workers' hours, raising prices for families, or limiting the care hours they offer to Medicaid clients, which could reduce access to care for some seniors and people with disabilities.

Families who directly employ a caregiver — a common arrangement for people needing around-the-clock help — would take on wage-and-hour obligations they do not have today, and casual babysitting is the only arrangement the bill leaves exempt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and significant: a workforce that performs intimate, physically demanding care is currently allowed to be paid below minimum wage with no overtime, and extending basic wage-floor protections to them is the kind of rule nearly every other covered worker already has. The main cost — higher prices for care and pressure on Medicaid budgets — is genuine, especially since public programs fund most paid home care, but it is the ordinary cost of complying with wage laws that other employers already bear. The bill is narrowly drafted, keeping casual babysitters exempt, which limits the burden on ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee on March 12, 2026, and the committee has not scheduled a hearing or a vote on it; with Congress still in session, it is sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, with 57 original cosponsors and a total of 83 Democratic cosponsors, all from the House Democratic caucus.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which has sole jurisdiction over amendments to the Fair Labor Standards Act.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history, which lists only the introduction and the committee referral.

The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to strike the exemptions that currently allow home care workers and providers of companionship services to be paid without minimum wage or overtime protections.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled in committee, home care agencies and their clients' payers continue operating under the exemption, so agencies keep the current cost structure and care workers keep waiting for minimum wage and overtime rights. No one has yet gained or lost materially from the bill itself; the status quo persists.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home care agencies keeping the status quo

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 57 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 12, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat — 83 of 217 House Democrats signed on and no Republican did — and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the 223-member Republican majority, which has not acted on it.

industries.note: Agencies currently employ aides under the companionship exemption and are not required to pay overtime or, in some arrangements, minimum wage. The bill would make them pay wage-and-hour compliant wages, a direct cost to their payroll that falls on them and the programs and families that fund care.

industries.industry: Medicaid and public home care programs
industries.note: Public programs fund most paid home care, so higher worker wages would raise program costs and could squeeze state budgets or reduce authorized care hours. Workers' gains and program costs pull in opposite directions.

industries.industry: Casual babysitters and the households that hire them
industries.note: The bill narrows the exemption so that only occasional babysitting by non-professionals stays exempt; occasional sitters are unaffected, so ordinary families hiring a sitter face no new obligations.

analysis.trajectory: A wage-and-hour bill with no Republican cosponsors has essentially no path in a House committee run by the Republican majority, and it has received no action since referral. The likely outcome is that it sits in committee until the Congress ends in January 2027 without a hearing or vote, unless Democrats take control in the November 2026 elections and a successor bill is reintroduced.
